title: Eating at Your Family's or In-Laws' House: How to Watch What You Eat Without Hurting Anyone's Feelings
intro: You don't need to refuse every dish to watch what you eat at your family's or in-laws' house. Take a little of everything, eat calmly, and show that you appreciate their cooking.

sections.h: Take a little first, add later
sections.p: Start with a moderate plate. Taste all the dishes served, but a little at a time. If you're still hungry, then add more. This looks polite and you won't overeat without realising.

Fill half your plate with vegetables and ulam. Take one piece of protein lauk like chicken, fish or meat. For rice, about one moderate scoop. Santan gravy is fine, just take it by the spoonful, not flooding the plate.

Try a line like 'So sedap, Mak, I'm full already. Can I tapau a bit for later?' Praise the cooking first, then decline. Most mums and in-laws are happy when their cooking is praised, not when your plate is full.

sections.h: Kuih and sweet drinks at tea time
sections.p: Afternoon tea usually has kuih and sweet tea. Pick the one kuih you like most and eat it slowly. For drinks, ask for less sweet, or drink half a cup of tea.

If you're bringing a dish, choose something light like stir-fried vegetables, grilled chicken or steamed fish. It looks like a normal contribution. At least there's one option you're comfortable eating more of.

action: This week, try filling half your plate with vegetables or ulam every time you eat at your family's house.
Memorise one polite line to decline more rice, starting with a compliment.
Pick only one kuih at tea time and enjoy it slowly.
Bring one light dish when you go back to your family's house this weekend.
Walk for 10-15 minutes with your family after eating, for example take your nieces and nephews to the park.
myth: Many think one meal at the in-laws' house ruins their diet. Actually, one or two meals don't decide your results. What matters is your eating pattern throughout the week.

faq.q: My in-laws get hurt if I don't take more rice. What should I do?
faq.a: Sincerely praise the cooking and ask to tapau a little for tomorrow. Most people are happier when their cooking is appreciated than when your plate is full.

faq.q: Should I not eat at all before going to my family's house?
faq.a: No need. Arriving very hungry usually makes us eat more. Have breakfast or a light protein snack like a boiled egg before you go.

faq.q: What if there's a kenduri or big family meal every week?
faq.a: Treat it as part of your routine. Watch what you eat on normal days, and on kenduri days focus on vegetables, protein lauk and moderate rice. It doesn't have to be perfect every time.
